query: For lightweight high-entropy alloys intended for weight-critical aerospace and rail-transport applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability—or inability—to combine low density with mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and high-temperature oxidation resistance? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, the observations predicted relative to a baseline alloy, the conditions under which the hypothesis should cease to hold, the existing observations that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Lightweight high-entropy alloys with an average atomic‐size mismatch δ below 6% form and retain a single‐phase solid solution microstructure, which (1) refines grain size to enhance mechanical strength, (2) supplies uniformly distributed Al and Cr to form continuous protective oxide and passive films, and thus (3) enables the simultaneous combination of low density with high strength, corrosion resistance, and high‐temperature oxidation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic lightweight HEA composed of Ti, V, Cr, Al, and Nb engineered to yield δ<6% in the as‐cast, homogenized condition.
generation.intervention: Adjust composition by substituting 5 at.% Ti with 5 at.% Cr to raise δ above 6% while keeping overall chemistry and density nearly constant.
generation.conditions: Room‐temperature tensile and hardness testing; corrosion testing in 3.5 wt% NaCl at ambient temperature; isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C in air for up to 100 h.
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of single‐phase solid solution versus precipitation of intermetallic phases.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy at δ<6% suppresses intermetallic formation, stabilizes fine grains (grain‐boundary strengthening), and maintains a uniform reservoir of Al/Cr that forms adherent Al₂O₃/Cr₂O₃ scales and passive films. When δ>6%, phase separation and intermetallics coarsen the microstructure, embrittle the alloy, and deplete Al/Cr, degrading corrosion and oxidation resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the δ>6% alloy baseline, the δ<6% alloy will show ≥10% higher yield strength, ≥20% higher hardness, ≥50% lower corrosion current density in 3.5% NaCl, and ≥30% lower oxide weight gain after 100 h at 1000 °C.
generation.baseline: The δ>6% composition (identical overall density, but containing intermetallic precipitates under the same heat‐treatment).
generation.boundary: At temperatures above ~1200 °C, rapid grain growth and scale breakdown will occur regardless of δ; in highly aggressive halide‐rich environments (e.g., HCl vapor), pitting will dominate and override the δ‐dependent passive film stability.
generation.uncertainty: Moderate—empirical studies on the precise δ threshold in lightweight HEAs are limited, and exact effect sizes may vary with processing history.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two HEA batches differing only by the 5 at.% Ti→Cr substitution (δ<6% vs δ>6%), apply identical casting, homogenization, and thermo‐mechanical processing, then subject both to mechanical, electrochemical, and oxidation tests under the stated conditions.
measurements: X-ray diffraction and TEM for phase analysis
Potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5% NaCl for corrosion current density
Thermogravimetric analysis of mass gain during 100 h at 1000 °C in air
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the δ>6% alloy matches or exceeds the δ<6% alloy in yield strength, hardness, corrosion current density, and oxidation weight gain under the same conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.
